title: Handling Missing Data III - Categorical Imputation
abstract:
Categorical columns cannot be filled with a mean or a median — neither
quantity exists for text. The notes give two techniques: fill by the most
frequent value (the mode), and, when more than 10% is missing, create a new
category called "Missing". This document covers both, the threshold rule that
separates them and where it comes from, the distortion mode imputation causes to
the category distribution, the interaction with one-hot encoding, and the
unseen-category problem that appears at serving time.

blocks.t: Why Categorical Columns Are Different
From the notes

Fill by most frequent value — e.g. fill by Mode = "Mumbai".
Mean or median are not possible.

There is no arithmetic on categories. The mean of {Mumbai, Delhi, Pune} is
undefined, and so is the median unless the categories are ordinal. The only
central-tendency statistic that exists for nominal data is the mode —
the most frequently occurring value.
Ordinal columns have one more option

If the categories are ordered — HS $<$ UG $<$ PG, or Low $<$ Med $<$ High —
the median category does exist and is often a better choice than the mode,
because it respects the ordering. Encode to integers first (Topic 15), impute the
median, then decode.
Technique 1 — Mode Imputation

Replace every missing value with the most frequent category. It is the direct
analogue of mean imputation, and it has the direct analogue of mean imputation's
problem.

blocks.cap:
The same city column at three missing rates. Every imputed row is
 assigned to Mumbai, so Mumbai's share grows while every other category's share
 shrinks. At 5% the distortion is tolerable; at 45% the distribution has been
 rewritten.

blocks.t: Exactly how much the distribution is distorted

Let category $c$ have true proportion $p_c$, let $m$ be the mode, and let a
fraction $f$ be missing completely at random. After mode imputation:

More simply: every non-mode category is multiplied by $(1-f)$, and all the lost
mass is added to the mode. With $p_{\text{Mumbai}}=0.42$ and $f=0.45$, Mumbai's
share rises to $0.42(0.55)+0.45 = 0.68$ — from a plurality to a large majority,
purely as an artefact.
The downstream consequences

items:
Rare categories are crushed. A category at 3% becomes 1.6% at
 $f=0.45$ — possibly below the threshold where a model can learn anything
 about it.

Association is weakened. The imputed rows all share one category
 while retaining their true values on every other column, so any
 chi-square or Cram\'er's V with the target is attenuated.

One-hot encoding amplifies it. The mode's dummy column becomes
 the dominant feature and may absorb the effect of missingness itself.

blocks.t: Technique 2 — Missing Category Imputation
From the notes

If more than 10% missing, create a new category. Replace NA with
"Missing" = a new category.

Instead of guessing, you declare ignorance explicitly. "Missing" becomes a
legitimate category alongside Mumbai and Delhi, gets its own one-hot column, and
the model learns its own effect for it.

blocks.cap:
Why the 10% rule exists. Below roughly 10%, mode imputation shifts
 the majority share and the entropy only slightly. Above it, both move sharply
 — you are no longer filling gaps, you are inventing a distribution.

blocks.t: The argument for "Missing" being the better default

Mode imputation asserts a fact you do not have — that this customer is from
Mumbai. The "Missing" category asserts only what you do know: that the value was
absent. It is honest, it costs one extra dummy column, and it preserves the
absence as information the model can exploit.

For categorical data this is strictly stronger than the missing-indicator trick
of Topic 24, because the indicator is built into the encoding — no extra
column is needed, and it cannot be accidentally dropped.

blocks.t: The Serving-Time Problem
Unseen categories are the categorical analogue of missing values

At inference a request arrives with city = "Chennai", which never appeared
in training. This is not technically a missing value, but it has the same effect:
the encoder has no column for it. Handle both cases together:

items:
OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore") so unseen categories
 encode as all-zeros rather than raising;

or route both into the same "Missing" / "other" bucket, so
 the model has one consistent rule for "I do not recognise this".

blocks.t:
The third option is usually best, because it gives unseen and absent values the
same learned effect rather than leaving unseen values with no representation at
all.
Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, OrdinalEncoder
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, GridSearchCV

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 4000
cities = ["Mumbai", "Delhi", "Pune", "Kochi", "Jaipur"]
p = [.42, .24, .16, .11, .07]
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "city":      rng.choice(cities, n, p=p),
    "education": rng.choice(["HS", "UG", "PG"], n, p=[.4, .4, .2]),   # ORDINAL
    "age":       rng.uniform(20, 65, n),
})
# missingness that DEPENDS on the city -> informative, i.e. MAR/MNAR
miss = rng.random(n) < np.where(df.city.isin(["Kochi", "Jaipur"]), .55, .10)
df.loc[miss, "city"] = np.nan
y = (miss * 0.9 + (df.age > 45) * 0.4 + rng.normal(0, .5, n) > .8).astype(int)

print(f"city missing: {df.city.isna().mean():.1%}")

# =====================================================================
# 1. WHY MEAN/MEDIAN ARE NOT POSSIBLE
# =====================================================================
try:
    df.city.mean()
except TypeError as e:
    print("mean of a category:", type(e).__name__)
print("mode exists:", df.city.mode()[0])       # 'Mumbai'

# =====================================================================
# 2. MODE IMPUTATION -- and the distortion it causes
# =====================================================================
mode_imp = SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")
filled = pd.Series(mode_imp.fit_transform(df[["city"]]).ravel())

comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    "true":       df.city.value_counts(normalize=True, dropna=True),
    "after_mode": filled.value_counts(normalize=True),
}).fillna(0).round(3)
comparison["change"] = (comparison.after_mode - comparison.true).round(3)
print(comparison)
#          true  after_mode  change
# Mumbai  0.462       0.594  +0.132   <- inflated
# Jaipur  0.043       0.033  -0.010   <- crushed

f = df.city.isna().mean()
pm = df.city.value_counts(normalize=True).iloc[0]
print(f"predicted mode share: {pm*(1-f)+f:.3f}   observed: "
      f"{filled.value_counts(normalize=True).iloc[0]:.3f}")

# Association with the target is ATTENUATED:
def cramers_v(a, b):
    ct = pd.crosstab(a, b)
    chi2 = stats.chi2_contingency(ct)[0]
    return np.sqrt(chi2 / (len(a) * (min(ct.shape) - 1)))

obs_mask = df.city.notna()
print("Cramer's V on observed rows only:",
      round(cramers_v(df.city[obs_mask], y[obs_mask]), 3))
print("Cramer's V after mode imputation:",
      round(cramers_v(filled, y), 3))

# =====================================================================
# 3. MISSING CATEGORY IMPUTATION -- the notes' >10% rule
# =====================================================================
MISSING_THRESHOLD = 0.10

def choose_strategy(s: pd.Series) -> str:
    rate = s.isna().mean()
    return ("most_frequent" if rate < MISSING_THRESHOLD else "constant")

print(f"\ncity is {df.city.isna().mean():.1%} missing "
      f"-> strategy = {choose_strategy(df.city)}")

missing_imp = SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value="Missing")
filled2 = pd.Series(missing_imp.fit_transform(df[["city"]]).ravel())
print(filled2.value_counts(normalize=True).round(3))
# 'Missing' is now a category in its own right -- 21% of the data.

# The observed categories keep their TRUE relative proportions:
obs_only = filled2[filled2 != "Missing"].value_counts(normalize=True)
true_only = df.city.value_counts(normalize=True)
print("\nrelative proportions preserved:",
      np.allclose(obs_only.sort_index(), true_only.sort_index()))

# =====================================================================
# 4. IS THE ABSENCE INFORMATIVE? -- the test that decides the strategy
# =====================================================================
print("\ntarget rate | city present:", y[~miss].mean().round(3))
print("target rate | city missing:", y[miss].mean().round(3))
chi2, pval = stats.chi2_contingency(pd.crosstab(miss, y))[:2]
print(f"chi-square p = {pval:.2e}",
      "-> ABSENCE IS INFORMATIVE, use 'Missing'" if pval < .01 else "-> not informative")

# =====================================================================
# 5. ORDINAL COLUMNS -- the median category DOES exist
# =====================================================================
edu = df.education.copy()
edu[rng.random(n) < .12] = np.nan
order = ["HS", "UG", "PG"]

codes = pd.Series(pd.Categorical(edu, categories=order, ordered=True).codes,
                  dtype="float")
codes[codes < 0] = np.nan
median_code = int(codes.median())
edu_median = edu.fillna(order[median_code])
print(f"\nordinal median category: {order[median_code]}  "
      f"(mode would be {edu.mode()[0]})")
# For ordered categories the median respects the ordering; the mode does not.

# =====================================================================
# 6. COMPARE THE STRATEGIES PROPERLY
# =====================================================================
X = df[["city", "age"]]

def make(strategy, fill=None, drop_first=True):
    return Pipeline([
        ("pre", ColumnTransformer([
            ("cat", Pipeline([
                ("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy=strategy, fill_value=fill)),
                ("ohe", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore",
                                      drop="first" if drop_first else None)),
            ]), ["city"]),
            ("num", "passthrough", ["age"]),
        ])),
        ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
    ])

for name, pipe in [
    ("mode",                make("most_frequent")),
    ("'Missing' category",  make("constant", "Missing")),
]:
    s = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc")
    print(f"{name:22s} cv auc {s.mean():.4f} +/- {s.std():.4f}")
# 'Missing' wins clearly here, because the absence IS the signal.

# =====================================================================
# 7. LET GRIDSEARCH DECIDE
# =====================================================================
gs = GridSearchCV(make("constant", "Missing"), {
    "pre__cat__imp__strategy":   ["most_frequent", "constant"],
    "pre__cat__imp__fill_value": ["Missing"],
    "clf__C":                    [0.1, 1.0, 10.0],
}, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1).fit(X, y)
print("\nbest:", {k: v for k, v in gs.best_params_.items() if "imp" in k},
      round(gs.best_score_, 4))

# =====================================================================
# 8. SERVING: MISSING *AND* UNSEEN, HANDLED THE SAME WAY
# =====================================================================
pipe = make("constant", "Missing").fit(X, y)

live = pd.DataFrame([
    {"city": "Mumbai",  "age": 34.0},     # known
    {"city": np.nan,    "age": 41.0},     # missing  -> 'Missing'
    {"city": "Chennai", "age": 29.0},     # UNSEEN   -> all-zero dummies
])
print("\nlive predictions:", pipe.predict_proba(live)[:, 1].round(3))

# Better: route unseen categories into the SAME bucket as missing,
# so they share a learned effect instead of encoding as nothing at all.
KNOWN = set(df.city.dropna().unique())
def normalise(frame):
    frame = frame.copy()
    frame["city"] = frame.city.where(frame.city.isin(KNOWN), "Missing")
    return frame
print("with unseen routed to 'Missing':",
      pipe.predict_proba(normalise(live))[:, 1].round(3))
Worked Examples
Mode imputation and the "Missing" category
Column city: Mumbai, Delhi, NaN, Mumbai, Chennai, Mumbai, NaN (7 rows, 2 missing).
Step 1 – frequencies of the observed values.
Step 2 – mode fill. The mode is Mumbai, so both NaNs become Mumbai. The category distribution shifts to Mumbai $= 5/7 \approx 71\%$, which inflates the most common class.
Step 3 – the alternative. If the missingness itself carries information (for example, people who skip the field are systematically from one city), create a new category instead:
\text{city} \in {\text{Mumbai, Delhi, Chennai, Missing}}
Now the model can learn from "Missing" rather than being biased toward Mumbai.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Categorical columns cannot use mean or median — those are not
 possible. The only central-tendency statistic is the mode.

Mode imputation: fill by the most frequent value.
 Simple, and appropriate when very little is missing.

It distorts the distribution: every non-mode category is
 multiplied by $(1-f)$ and all the lost mass goes to the mode. Rare
 categories get crushed and associations are attenuated.

Missing category imputation: if more than 10% is
 missing, create a new category — replace NA with
 "Missing".

The new category preserves the relative proportions of the observed
 categories and retains the absence as information — for
 categorical columns this replaces the missing-indicator trick entirely.

Test whether the absence is informative (compare the target rate for
 present vs missing rows). If it is, use "Missing" regardless of
 the rate.

For ordinal columns the median category exists and
 respects the ordering; prefer it to the mode.

At serving time, handle unseen categories the same way as
 missing ones — route both to "Missing", or use
 handle_unknown="ignore".

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. How do you impute a categorical column?

With the mode if very little is missing — under roughly 10%. Above that,
create an explicit "Missing" category. Mean and median do not exist for
nominal data.
Q. Why does mode imputation get worse as the missing rate rises?

Because every imputed row is assigned to the same category. The mode's share
grows by roughly $f(1-p_m)$ while every other category shrinks by a factor
$(1-f)$. At 45% missing you have rewritten the distribution rather than repaired
it.
Q. Why is a "Missing" category often better than the mode?

Because it is honest. Mode imputation asserts a fact you do not have; the
"Missing" category asserts only that the value was absent. It preserves
the observed categories' proportions and lets the model learn a separate effect
for absence — which under MAR or MNAR is frequently the strongest signal
available.
Q. How do you decide between them for a given column?

Two checks. First the missing rate against the 10% threshold. Second, and more
important: compare the target rate between rows where the value is present and
rows where it is missing. If they differ significantly, the absence is
informative and you should keep it as a category regardless of the rate.

Q. Your model crashes in production on city="Chennai". Why, and
what do you do?

The one-hot encoder has no column for an unseen category. Set
handle_unknown="ignore" so it encodes as all zeros, or — better — map
any unrecognised category into the same "Missing" bucket, so unseen and
absent values share a learned effect rather than one of them having no
representation.
Q. Does imputing a categorical column change the number of features?

Mode imputation does not. The "Missing" category adds exactly one column
after one-hot encoding — which is the price of retaining the information, and a
cheap one.
